items.question: What force pulls things down towards the Earth?
items.explanation: Gravity is the pull of the Earth on everything. It is why a ball falls when you drop it and why we don't float away. The Moon's gravity is weaker, about one-sixth of Earth's.

items.question: Your mass on the Moon is less than your mass on Earth.
items.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in you, and it stays the same everywhere. Your weight (the pull of gravity on you) is less on the Moon, about one-sixth. So you weigh less, but your mass does not change.

items.question: A car travels 100 m in 5 seconds. What is its speed?
items.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time. So 100 m ÷ 5 s = 20 metres per second. That is the same as 72 km per hour.

items.question: Near the Earth, a falling object speeds up by about ___ m/s every second (ignoring air).
items.explanation: This number is called the acceleration due to gravity, written as g. It means a falling stone gains about 9.8 m/s of speed every second. It is often rounded to 10 to make sums easier.

items.question: In a vacuum (no air at all), a feather and a hammer are dropped together from the same height. What happens?
options: They land at the same time
items.explanation: Gravity speeds up all objects by the same amount. On Earth, air slows the feather down. With no air, nothing slows it, so both land together.
items.funFact: Astronaut David Scott tried this on the Moon in 1971 — both landed together!
